summary: Extends the Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP) so a PCE can compute and set up Segment Routing paths in the IPv6 data plane, adding to existing support for the MPLS data plane.

eli5.summary: A navigation app picks a route, then tells the driver. This teaches the route-planning protocol to give directions for SRv6.

questions: what is the srv6 ero subobject
what is path setup type 3 in pcep
subtitle: The PCEP extensions that let a path computation server hand out Segment Routing paths for the IPv6 data plane.

tldr.problem: PCEP already supported Segment Routing for the MPLS data plane, but a PCE had no way to compute and deliver paths made of SRv6 segments.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds a new Path Setup Type (3), an SRv6-PCE-CAPABILITY sub-TLV for the OPEN exchange, and SRv6-ERO and SRv6-RRO subobjects that carry 128-bit SRv6 SIDs, with validation rules and error codes.
tldr.outcome: A controller acting as a PCE can instantiate SRv6 candidate paths on head-end nodes acting as PCCs. The RFC has since been updated by RFC 9756 and RFC 9933.

today: RFC 9603 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 9756 and RFC 9933, so read those alongside it. It builds on RFC 8664, which covers the MPLS data plane.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
In Segment Routing (SR), per RFC 8402, the source node steers a packet along a path given as an ordered list of instructions called segments. SR can use the MPLS or the IPv6 data plane. The Path Computation Element Communication Protocol (PCEP, RFC 5440) lets a Path Computation Client (PCC) and a Path Computation Element (PCE) talk about paths. RFC 8231 and RFC 8281 add stateful operation and PCE-initiated LSPs, and RFC 8664 adds SR for the MPLS data plane.

This document extends RFC 8664 to the IPv6 data plane (SRv6). A PCC can request an SRv6 path from a stateful or stateless PCE. The mechanism also lets a network controller acting as a PCE instantiate candidate paths of an SR Policy on a head-end node acting as a PCC. The RFC relies on the PATH-SETUP-TYPE TLV and procedures of RFC 8408.

In this context an SRv6 path is a list of IPv6 SIDs, and the "LSP" of the PCEP specifications corresponds to an SRv6 path.
sections.eli5: There was already a way to tell routers the path in one kind of network. This RFC adds the same thing for a second kind of network, the IPv6 one.

sections.title: Advertising SRv6 Capability
sections.content:
The RFC defines Path Setup Type (PST) 3, meaning the path is set up using SRv6. A PCEP speaker advertises support by listing PST 3 in the PATH-SETUP-TYPE-CAPABILITY TLV of its OPEN object, and then it MUST also include the new SRv6-PCE-CAPABILITY sub-TLV (type 27). Every RP or SRP object for an SRv6 path MUST carry a PATH-SETUP-TYPE TLV with PST 3. The formats of PCReq, PCRep, PCInitiate, PCRpt and PCUpd are not changed.

The sub-TLV has a Reserved field, a 2-octet Flags field with one defined bit, the N bit (bit position 14), and optional pairs of (MSD-Type, MSD-Value). A PCC sets N to 1 to say it can resolve a Node or Adjacency Identifier (NAI) to an SRv6 SID. The MSD pairs give the Maximum SID Depth, the SRv6 SID imposition limit of the sending PCC only. The flags and MSD pairs are meaningful only in an Open sent to a PCE.

A PCE MUST NOT send SRv6 paths that exceed the MSD of the PCC. A PCC that needs to change its MSD MUST close the session and re-establish it. During computation the PCE should also consider the MSD of every node along the path, learned for example through IGP or BGP-LS. The RFC recommends leaving MSD out of the sub-TLV when the PCE can already learn it that way.
sections.eli5: When two programs meet, they swap a card saying "I speak SRv6, and I can handle up to this many directions in one go."

sections.title: The SRv6-ERO Subobject
sections.content:
Routes travel in PCEP as an Explicit Route Object (ERO) made of subobjects. The new SRv6-ERO subobject (type 40) carries one SRv6 segment. Its main fields are the L flag (loose hop), Length, NAI Type (NT), Flags, a 16-bit Endpoint Behavior, an optional 128-bit SRv6 SID, an optional NAI and an optional SID Structure.

Three flag bits say which optional parts are present. S set means the SID is absent and the PCC picks it, for example by looking up the NAI, so the NAI must be present. F set means the NAI is absent, and it MUST be set when NT is 0. T set means an 8-byte SID Structure follows. The V bit requests SID verification per RFC 9256. The optional elements MUST appear in the order SID, NAI, SID Structure. If the L flag is zero, the PCC MUST NOT overwrite the SID.

The Endpoint Behavior is optional but recommended for maintainability and diagnostics. When the behavior is not known, the value 0xFFFF is used. A PCC reports the path it actually applied in a Reported Route Object (RRO) using SRv6-RRO subobjects, which have the same format without the L flag, and the V bit is ignored there.
sections.eli5: Each step of the route is a small card with the street address on it, and a few tick boxes that say which extra details are attached.

sections.title: NAI Types and SID Structure
sections.content:
The NAI identifies the node or adjacency a SID belongs to. NT value 0 means no NAI. Value 2 is an IPv6 node ID, value 4 is an IPv6 adjacency with a pair of global addresses, and value 6 is an IPv6 adjacency with link-local addresses, each in the formats defined in RFC 8664.

The optional SID Structure describes how a SID splits into parts, following RFC 8986: locator block, locator node, function and argument. It holds four 1-octet lengths (LB, LN, Fun. and Arg.) in bits, followed by Reserved and Flags (no flags currently defined). The four lengths must add up to at most 128 bits. If they add up to more, the SID is invalid and the receiver returns a PCErr with Error-Type 10 and Error-value 37 ("Invalid SRv6 SID Structure").

The RFC says the structure helps with operations and monitoring, such as checking conformance with an operator's SID allocation scheme. It says possible future uses, such as provisioning filtering rules at domain boundaries, are outside its scope.
sections.eli5: A long address has parts, like country, city and street. The structure tells how many digits belong to each part.

sections.title: Validation and Error Handling
sections.content:
A PCC that gets an SRv6-ERO MUST check that Length, the S, F and T bits and NT agree. A PCC that finds an inconsistency must treat the whole ERO as invalid and send a PCErr with Error-Type 10 and Error-value 11 ("Malformed object"). An unknown NT value yields Error-value 41. Both S and F set yields Error-value 42. A mix of SRv6-ERO and other subobject types yields Error-value 43. An SRv6 path that exceeds the PCC's MSD yields Error-value 40.

If a PCEP speaker receives PST 3 without the SRv6-PCE-CAPABILITY sub-TLV, it MUST send a PCErr with Error-Type 10 and Error-Value 34 and then close the session. If it receives the sub-TLV without PST 3 in the list, it ignores the sub-TLV. If the sub-TLV appears more than once, only the first is processed. Receiving an SRv6-ERO when the capability was not advertised yields Error-Type 19 and Error-value 19.

The segments in an ERO are interpreted in order: the first subobject is the first segment the traffic is directed to, and so on. Failure of a SID to verify is reported in the LSP-ERROR-CODE TLV with the value "SID Verification fails".
sections.eli5: If a card is filled out wrongly, the receiver sends it back with a note saying exactly what was wrong.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 5440, RFC 8231, RFC 8281, RFC 8253 and RFC 8664 apply, as does Section 2.5 of RFC 6952. Because this specification lets a controller instantiate SRv6 paths, a session without integrity protection lets an attacker create an SRv6 path that may escape further verification checks. The MSD in the Open message could also disclose forwarding capabilities.

The RFC therefore says that securing the PCEP session with TLS is RECOMMENDED.
sections.eli5: If anyone could send directions to the routers, they could send traffic the wrong way. Locking the conversation with a secret code prevents that.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA assigned the following values and created new registries for this work. The SRv6-ERO subobject is type 40 in the ERO registry, and the SRv6-RRO subobject is type 40 in the route record registry. The SRv6-PCE-CAPABILITY sub-TLV is type 27, and Path Setup Type 3 is added to the "PCEP Path Setup Types" registry.

New registries are "PCEP SRv6-ERO NAI Types" (4-bit NT, IETF Review), "SRv6-ERO Flag Field" (12 bits, Standards Action) and "SRv6 Capability Flag Field" (16 bits, Standards Action). The RFC also adds LSP-ERROR-CODE value 10 and new PCEP error values.
sections.eli5: The numbers used in the messages are written in an official list so nobody picks the same number for something else.

fields.desc: Zero on send, ignored on receipt.

fields.desc: Behavior of the SID; 0xFFFF if unknown.

fields.desc: The 128-bit segment identifier, present unless S is set.
